segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One day, as he was teaching the people in the temple and proclaiming the good news, the chief priests and the scribes came up with the elders,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Tell us, by what authority are you doing these things? Or who is it that gave you this authority?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I too will ask you a question, and you tell me:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Was John’s baptism from heaven or from human beings?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They reasoned it out among themselves, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why did you not believe him?’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But if we say, ‘From human beings,’ all the people will stone us, for they are convinced that John was a prophet.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they answered that they did not know where it was from.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Nor am I telling you by what authority I am doing these things.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he began to tell the people this parable:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “A man planted a vineyard, leased it to tenants, and went abroad for a long time.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: When the time came, he sent a slave to the tenants, so that they would give him some of the fruit of the vineyard. But the tenants beat him and sent him away empty-handed.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He went on to send another slave; but that one too they beat and humiliated and sent away empty-handed.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He went on to send a third; this one too they wounded and threw out.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then the owner of the vineyard said, ‘What shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps they will respect him.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But when the tenants saw him, they reasoned with one another, saying, ‘This is the heir. Let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He will come and destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they heard this, they said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “May that never happen!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he looked straight at them and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What then is this that is written: ‘The stone that the builders rejected, this has become the cornerstone’?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces; and anyone it falls on, it will crush.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The scribes and the chief priests sought to lay hands on him that very hour, but they feared the people; for they knew that he had told this parable against them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they watched him closely and sent spies who pretended to be righteous, so that they might catch him in something he said and so hand him over to the rule and authority of the governor.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They questioned him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly and show no partiality, but truly teach the way of God.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Is it lawful for us to give tribute to Caesar, or not?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he saw through their craftiness and said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Show me a denarius. Whose image and inscription does it have?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Caesar’s.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Then give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they were unable to catch him in what he said in front of the people; and, amazed at his answer, they fell silent.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then some of the Sadducees, who deny that there is a resurrection, came up and questioned him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies having a wife, and he is childless, his brother should take the wife and raise up offspring for his brother.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Now there were seven brothers. The first took a wife and died childless;

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: then the second

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and the third took her, and in the same way all seven left no children and died.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Last of all, the woman died too.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So in the resurrection, whose wife does the woman become? For all seven had her as wife.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The children of this age marry and are given in marriage,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but those who are counted worthy to attain to that age and to the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For they can no longer die either, because they are equal to angels, and they are children of God, being children of the resurrection.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But that the dead are raised, even Moses made known in the passage about the bush, where he calls the Lord the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He is not God of the dead but of the living, for to him all are alive.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some of the scribes answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Teacher, you have spoken well.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For they no longer dared to ask him anything.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “How is it that they say the Messiah is David’s son?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For David himself says in the book of Psalms, ‘The Lord said to my Lord: “Sit at my right hand

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.”’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So David calls him ‘Lord’; how then is he his son?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While all the people were listening, he said to the disciples,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes and love greetings in the marketplaces and the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at dinners,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: who devour widows’ houses and for show make long prayers. These will receive a heavier judgment.”

notes.note: The Greek word denotes a person owned by a master, not a hired employee. Older English versions say 'servant'; several modern translations now use 'slave', as here. A landowner sending his slaves as agents was ordinary practice, and their mistreatment was an insult to the owner himself.

The quotation is Psalm 118:22, and the Greek is literally 'head of the corner'. It may mean a foundation stone at the corner of a building or the capstone that completes it at the top; scholars are divided. Either way it is the most important stone, which the builders had thrown aside.

notes.traditional: it will grind him to powder
notes.note: The verb ordinarily means to winnow, scattering chaff to the wind, so the sense may be 'it will scatter him like chaff'. In one Greek version of Daniel 2:44 it is used of a kingdom that crushes all others, in a passage about a stone, and most translators take that sense here.

This was the direct tax Rome levied on subject peoples, imposed on Judea when it came under a Roman governor. Its introduction had provoked an uprising, and it remained a bitter issue. A plain yes would discredit Jesus with the people, and a plain no could be reported to the governor as sedition.

A Roman silver coin, roughly a day's wage for a labourer. It carried the emperor's portrait and titles, which under Tiberius included the claim to be son of the divine Augustus. Many Jews found such coins offensive, since they bore both an image and a claim to divinity.

The questioners asked whether it is lawful to 'give' tribute; Jesus answers with a compound of the same verb that means to give back or pay what is owed. 'Render' in the traditional versions meant this but no longer conveys it. The change of verb implies that the coin already belongs to Caesar, and leaves open what belongs to God.

notes.phrase: raise up offspring for his brother
notes.traditional: raise up seed unto his brother
notes.note: The reference is to the law in Deuteronomy 25:5–6, under which a dead man's brother married the widow and the first son counted as the dead man's heir. The Sadducees use it to make resurrection look absurd.

notes.traditional: children of this world / sons of this age
notes.note: The Greek is literally 'sons of this age', a Semitic idiom in which 'son of' means 'belonging to'. The same idiom lies behind 'children of God' and 'children of the resurrection' in verse 36. 'This age' and 'that age' reflect the Jewish division of time into the present age and the age to come.

notes.phrase: in the passage about the bush
notes.note: The Greek says only 'at the bush'. Before chapter and verse numbers existed, a passage was cited by naming its subject; this is the story of the burning bush in Exodus 3. The Sadducees accepted the books of Moses as authoritative, so Jesus argues from them.

The Greek is a bare dative, 'all live to him'. It may mean that from God's standpoint all are alive, as rendered here, or that all live for him or by his power. The argument is that God would not name himself as the God of people who had ceased to exist.

The Greek christos means 'anointed' and translates the Hebrew word that gives English 'Messiah', the title of the king Israel expected. Here the title itself is under discussion, so it is rendered 'Messiah'; where the word functions as a name for Jesus, this translation keeps 'Christ'. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

notes.phrase: The Lord said to my Lord
notes.traditional: The LORD said unto my Lord
notes.note: The quotation is Psalm 110:1. The Hebrew has two different words, the divine name and 'my lord', a term for a superior; the Greek uses the same word for both. Jesus' question turns on the second: David, the supposed speaker, calls the Messiah his lord, which a father would not normally say of his son.

candidates.reason: Translators split between 'slave' and 'servant' across the parables and Paul's self-descriptions, and a reader would be misled if the word varied from chapter to chapter.
It recurs throughout the Gospels and Acts; 'scribe' suggests a copyist to modern readers, where 'legal scholar' or 'teacher of the law' are plausible alternatives, so one choice is needed.
It is rendered variously 'age', 'world' and 'eternity' across the New Testament, and the this-age/that-age contrast needs one consistent treatment.
It is frequent in Luke–Acts and Paul, and 'preach the gospel', 'proclaim the good news' and 'bring good news' should not alternate at random.
It ranges over 'authority', 'power', 'right' and 'jurisdiction' across the New Testament and needs a default with defined alternates.
